approved: Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2018 Measures No. 1) Bill 2018
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill introduces a mandatory scheme requiring sponsors of certain medicines to report shortages or permanent discontinuations to the Department of Health Secretary.
It creates penalties for non-compliance and makes miscellaneous amendments to improve regulatory efficiency, such as supporting online forms and clarifying requirements.

Sponsors must report critical-impact shortages within 2 working days, other shortages within 10 working days, critical discontinuations at least 12 months ahead, and other discontinuations at least 6 months ahead.
Introduce a mandatory reporting scheme for medicine shortages and permanent discontinuations.
Create civil penalties for non-compliance with reporting requirements.
Make miscellaneous amendments to reduce inefficiencies in therapeutic goods regulation.
Sponsors of prescription medicines, medicines on a Medicines Watch List, and other medicines determined by the Minister for Health, as well as industry and the Therapeutic Goods Administration.

The bill introduces a mandatory reporting scheme for medicine shortages to the Therapeutic Goods Administration, requiring sponsors to report critical shortages within two working days and all others within ten, with civil penalties for non-compliance, and establishes a Medicines Watch List for medicines whose shortage would critically impact patient care.

The bill introduces mandatory reporting for medicine shortages and discontinuations, with notification timeframes from two working days for critical shortages to at least 12 months for critical discontinuations, and civil penalties focused on educating non-compliant suppliers. It also includes miscellaneous amendments to streamline standards, the Special Access Scheme, and marketing approval variations, with Labor supporting the legislation as in the public interest.

The speaker supported the Therapeutic Goods Amendment Bill 2018, which introduces mandatory reporting of medicine shortages and penalties for noncompliance. They cited shortages of methylphenidate (Ritalin), amiloride, vancomycin, metronidazole, and norfloxacin, and noted the decline of Australian pharmaceutical manufacturing and consolidation of multinational companies.

The bill is supported but does not go far enough; the speaker urged stronger regulation to prevent shortages of essential medicines, including broad-spectrum antibiotics, vaccines, EpiPens, and medications for epilepsy, asthma, and diabetes.

The speaker supported the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2018 Measures No. 1) Bill 2018, which introduces mandatory reporting of shortages and permanent discontinuations of high-risk medicines, with civil penalties for noncompliance, citing widespread failures in the existing voluntary scheme—such as the EpiPen shortage not being reported for two months—and referencing a Society of Hospital Pharmacists of Australia survey that found 85% of shortages were not listed by suppliers and that shortages had directly impacted patient care in 32% of cases.

The speaker argued for the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2018 Measures No. 1) Bill, which introduces mandatory reporting of medicine shortages and discontinuations for high-risk prescription medicines, with civil penalties for noncompliance. The bill was prompted by the ineffective voluntary scheme and shortages like the EpiPen, requiring critical-impact shortages to be reported within two working days.
